newsitem.title: USA: U.S. towns, counties deeply split on flow control.
newsitem.headline: U.S. towns, counties deeply split on flow control.

text.p: The nation's towns and counties expressed deep division on Tuesday on whether the U.S. Congress should enact legislation to protect billions of dollars of solid-waste facility debt.
Randy Johnson, president-elect of the National Association of Counties, Hennep implored a U.S. Senate Committee to protect flow control sites nationwide.

Johnson, chairman of Hennepin County, Minn.'s county commission, warned that $3.3 billion in facility debt nationwide already has been downgraded or put on credit watch by rating agencies since the U.S. Supreme Court struck down flow control in May 1994.

But a coalition of nearly 250 New Jersey mayors said flow control fees "play havoc" with their budgets, forcing them to divert badly needed funds for infrastructure, police and public safety to garbage disposal.

Their spokesman, Northvale, N.J. Mayor John Rooney, said the state's utilities have a "stranglehold" over towns like his, "forcing us to use their product and only their product." He called waste flow control a "garbage tax that feeds county utility authorities," which he described as "bureaucratic mononliths."
The local officials were testifying before the Senate Committee on Environmental and Public Works Committee, chaired by U.S. Sen. John Chafee, R-R.I.

U.S. Rep. Bill Pascrell, D-N.J., said he is "adamantly opposed" to flow control. The former Patterson, N.J. mayor said that Patterson spent $11 million out of a $137 million 1995 annual budget on waste disposal.

"Instead of passing flow control legislation, Congress should bury it in the trash heap of discarded ideas," Pascrell said. "It is a flawed policy that benefits neither consumer, taxpayer nor the general economy. It's only beneficiaries are local government officials and county utility authorities."

Pascrell charged that part of the $1.7 billion in bonds issued by New Jersey counties to construct waste disposal facilities "has allowed certain counties to bond for facilities that were never built."
"Imagine bonding for a capital facility that was never built? That debt is important. That debt is not going to go away," he said.
Committee Chairman John Chaffee shot back, "Wait. They bonded to build a facility and you say they never built it?"
"What did they do with the money?" Chafee asked.
"You need another hearing for that," Pascrell said, refusing to comment. "This is the wrong committee," he said. Pascrell was not asked to name localities.

U.S. Rep. Bob Franks, a New Jersey Republican, warned that if Congress does not step in with flow control legislation this year, "taxpayers will face huge increases in their local property tax bills."

Pascrell conceded that he "possibly" would support some form of flow control legislation that protects, or "grandfathers," some existing flow control sites. "It's obvious that we want to compromise. It's in everybody's interest."
Flow controil refers to the abililty of local governments to direct solid waste to specific facilities that are financed by tax-exempt bonds.
The U.S. Supreme Court in 1994 said that flow control violates the interstate commerce clause of the U.S. Constitution.
